Lease or buy a car: compare costs at the same exit date

Five graphics compare recurring payments, full-term lease costs, a purchase-loan payoff, resale proceeds and the cash needed before exit.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a lease return with buying and selling at the same date

Interactive planning lab

Buy-and-sell net cash cost at the common date$28,046.24
Lease-and-return cash cost over the full term$28,900
Lease cost minus buy-and-sell cost$853.76

Hypothetical full-term comparison ending with no vehicle owned and no purchase-loan balance: the purchased car is sold and remaining principal paid; the leased car is returned. Price and lease payment are all-in quote inputs, with no tax calculation. Purchase down payment is capped at price. The loan uses constant nominal annual interest divided by twelve, monthly payments and unrounded intermediate amounts; payments stop at payoff. Lease signing cash excludes monthly instalments and refundable deposits; instalments arrive at month-end in the model. Return charges are separately entered. Sale proceeds are net of selling and loan-closure charges but before repaying principal. Identical operating costs cancel; selected additional monthly costs are included for each option. No lease buyout, residual-value shortfall guarantee beyond entered charges, early termination, refundable deposit, approval, mileage forecast, discounting or investment return is modeled.

The central idea

A fair terminal comparison needs the same ending position. Here the leased car is returned and the purchased car is sold with its remaining loan repaid.

01

Compare a full-term return with a purchase followed by sale

A lower monthly lease payment does not settle the total-cost question. The purchase option can leave both an asset and a loan, while the lease contract can require a different ending transaction.

The Vehicle Sales Authority of British Columbia’s financing and leasing guide emphasizes understanding the total obligation, taxes, fees and ending conditions. The FCAC’s car-financing overview also separates financing choices from their risks.

This model assumes comparable vehicles and a forty-eight-month lease. At that date, the leased car is returned, while the purchased car is sold and its remaining principal repaid. Both choices then leave no vehicle and no purchase-loan balance. Keeping the owned car or buying out the lease would require a different comparison.

02

Trace the purchase price, down payment and loan

The hypothetical all-in purchase price is CAD 42,000. A CAD 5,000 down payment leaves CAD 37,000 financed over sixty months at a constant 6% nominal annual rate divided by twelve.

The calculated loan payment is approximately CAD 715.31. Additional buyer costs are CAD 50 monthly, making the first recurring commitment about CAD 765.31. Identical operating costs common to both choices are omitted; differences must be entered separately.

After forty-eight payments, about CAD 8,311.18 of principal remains. The model’s net sale proceeds before debt repayment are CAD 22,000, leaving roughly CAD 13,689 of terminal equity after that principal is paid. Sale proceeds should already reflect selling and loan-closure charges, without subtracting the principal twice.

03

Reconcile the buy-and-sell cost without adding the price twice

The purchase waterfall adds the applied down payment, loan payments within the window, additional running costs and remaining principal paid at sale. It then subtracts the net sale proceeds before debt.

The resulting cost is CAD 28,046.24. Down payment plus loan payments plus final principal equals purchase price plus interest, so adding the purchase price again would double-count the financed portion.

The down payment is capped at price; a larger requested amount is not treated as spent. Loan payments stop at payoff if the selected loan period is shorter than the lease term. Intermediate amounts are unrounded until display, so an actual quoted payment schedule can differ slightly.

04

Include the full lease obligation and its return charges

The lease example pays CAD 2,000 at signing, CAD 550 a month for forty-eight months and CAD 500 of entered return charges. No additional lessee running costs are selected. The full cash cost is CAD 28,900.

Signing cash excludes monthly instalments and refundable deposits in this model. If a real quote includes the first instalment at signing, separate it so it is not counted again in the monthly stream. No tax rate or lease financing rate is inferred from the quote.

The car is assumed returned with no buyout and no residual-value obligation beyond the entered charges. That is a specific contract assumption. Confirm distance, wear, administration and other obligations; early termination and refundable deposits are outside this comparison.

05

Read the terminal saving alongside the earlier cash commitment

Under the defaults, lease cost minus buy-and-sell cost is positive CAD 853.76, so buying and selling has the lower modeled net cost. That result depends on the entered sale proceeds, payment quotes and extra costs.

The cumulative cash chart shows why this does not automatically make buying easier to fund. Purchase payments are higher before the final sale credit arrives. If the sale proceeds fall below remaining principal, the shortfall needs other cash at closing; it is not forgiven by selling the car.

The matrix varies net resale proceeds and the monthly lease quote. Positive cells mean the lease costs more; negative cells favor it on this arithmetic. The model assigns no resale probability and discounts no cash flow. Review affordability and contract flexibility as well as the full-term total before committing.

Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
